To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the maximum voluntary joint moment can be accurately predicted as a function of angular velocity using a model that includes differential activation.
the maximum voluntary knee torque that can be generated is the product of the maximum torque that can be produced by the muscle and the maximum voluntary level of muscle activation.
the maximum voluntary knee extension torque is a non-hyperbola and this is because of differential muscle activation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the modelling of human movement and the development of a model to calculate the torque exerted by a joint as a function of angular velocity.
the development and application of a model of the maximum voluntary joint torques/angular velocity relationship.
the relationship between joint torque and angular velocity during human movement.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

differential activation of the muscle is a major factor in explaining the torque-angular velocity relationship during maximum voluntary contractions and that this factor should be included when developing mathematical models of muscle force production.
the torque-velocity relationship is a function of both the maximum tetanic force and the differential activation of the muscle.
differential activation accounts for the maximum voluntary joint torques in human movement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a model of joint torque that is based on the assumption of a hyperbolic torque/angular velocity relationship is not adequate to explain the data obtained from human movement.

the maximum torque that can be produced by the knee extensors is a function of angular velocity, with the relationship between maximum torque and angular velocity being hyperbolic at low angular velocities and non-hyperbolaic at high angular velocities.
the torque/velocity relationship for a joint may be modelled as a product of two functions: the tetanic torque/angular relationship and the activation/velocity relationship.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the maximum voluntary torque is a function of both the maximum voluntary activation and the maximum voluntary torque.
the maximum torque that can be developed by the knee extensors is not a simple function of knee angular velocities, but rather depends on the activation level of the muscle at each angular velocity.
differential activation should not be ignored when modelling maximum voluntary movements.
